# Locating the Wiper Relay and Control Module on a 1994–1998 Ford Mustang

When troubleshooting an electrical fault like zero voltage reaching the wiper motor, the first step is often verifying fuse integrity. If fuses are confirmed good yet no current reaches the actuator, the issue usually lies in the control logic or power distribution relay circuit. On Ford vehicles manufactured between 1994 and 1998, specifically those equipped with the 3.0L V6 or the more common 5.0L V8 engines, identifying the wiper system components requires understanding how they diverge from earlier model years.

The primary component to investigate is the windshield washer pump relay, which serves a dual purpose in this generation of Mustangs. Unlike newer vehicles with dedicated electronic control modules (ECMs) for every peripheral function, these older platforms often share relays or use a specific location that can be easily missed during inspection. The wiper and washer functions are frequently tied to the same relay housing under the hood.

To locate the component physically, you need to inspect the engine bay fuse box, which is mounted on the driver's side inner fender well, near the strut tower. Inside this plastic enclosure, you will find a bank of blade-style fuses and larger relays. The specific relay responsible for the wiper system is typically labeled "WIPER" or sometimes grouped with the washer function. In some configurations, particularly on models where the module was relocated from the dashboard to the engine compartment for easier access, this unit acts as the power switch that closes the circuit to the motor when the switch on the stalk is activated.

If your diagnostic check confirms voltage exists at the fuse input but not at the output wire leading to the wiper motor, the relay inside that housing has likely failed mechanically or internally shorted. The solution involves swapping the suspected relay with an identical one from another circuit in the same box—such as the horn or cooling fan relay—to test functionality without needing a multimeter immediately. This is a standard hardware debugging technique: isolate the variable by substitution before assuming the load (the motor) is dead.

However, there is a critical distinction to make regarding the 1994–1998 timeframe. Some variations of these Mustangs utilized an integrated wiper control module located inside the vehicle, typically mounted on the dashboard near the steering column or behind the instrument cluster. This module handled the timing logic for intermittent and mist modes. If your vehicle does not have a relay under the hood labeled "WIPER," or if replacing that relay yields no change in behavior, you must check the interior fuse panel located at the base of the driver's side kick panel.

Inside this interior box, look for a circuit breaker or a smaller, rectangular module specifically designated for wiper control. In these cases, the failure point is not the power relay but the logic board itself. If the module fails, it often results in total loss of all wiper functions regardless of the stalk position, and simply replacing the fuse will not restore operation because the internal circuitry has burned out.

When performing this repair, ensure you have a wiring diagram specific to your VIN year and trim level. Wiring harnesses can differ between GT and non-GT models, and pinout configurations for the relay sockets may vary slightly. Always verify that the new replacement relay matches the amperage rating of the original; using a lower-rated component could lead to premature failure under load again.

For developers accustomed to debugging software systems, this mechanical troubleshooting mirrors checking dependencies in a distributed system. You have confirmed the upstream service (fuses) is healthy, yet the downstream consumer (motor) receives no data (voltage). The intermediary controller (relay/module) is the single point of failure. Isolating that component through physical swapping or continuity testing resolves the root cause without requiring invasive teardowns unless the dashboard module proves intractable.
